title: CSV import through a staging table with validation
summary: Load the file as text into a staging table, compute typed values and a list of problems per row in one view, then move only the clean rows and report the rest with row numbers. COPY's ON_ERROR ignore is the quick alternative, and the example shows what it can't catch.

examples.title: Which casts you can trust with Turkish input

annotations.note: The same text is March 4 under MDY and April 3 under DMY, and 31.12.2026 is valid only under DMY. DateStyle's built-in default is ISO, MDY, but initdb sets it from the server's lc_time locale, so one import can mean different dates on two servers. Build YYYY-MM-DD yourself: ISO dates read the same under every DateStyle.

pg_input_is_valid and pg_input_error_info (PG 16) run the type's input check without raising an error, so nothing aborts. '1.250' passes: it is 1.25 to PostgreSQL and 1250 to a Turkish reader. Valid input isn't necessarily the value the user meant, so check the format first.

lower() follows the collation's case rules. Under the default ones I lowers to i, so KALDI becomes kaldi and matches neither spelling; tr-x-icu applies Turkish rules (I to ı, İ to i) and all three rows agree.

An ordinary cast has no soft mode: the error aborts the statement and the transaction, and this runner stops here the way psql does with ON_ERROR_STOP. COPY behaves the same by default, which is why the validation below never casts before checking.

examples.title: Stage as text, validate in one view, report, then move the clean rows

annotations.note: Text columns and no constraints: every line of the file lands, and the rules run afterwards, in SQL you can query. \copy with a column list leaves row_no out, so the identity numbers rows in the order COPY reads them: the numbers you report back. A quoted field with a line break makes rows and file lines differ.

Each CASE yields a reason or NULL, and array_remove drops the NULLs, so '{}' means clean. One row can collect several reasons (TC-5 has two), so the user fixes the file in one pass instead of one error per attempt.
The first and third rules repeat the target's foreign key and its CHECK (seconds >= 0). Left to the INSERT, the first violation would fail the whole statement, naming a constraint rather than a row.
The primary key, checked twice: against the file itself (both TC-7 rows are rejected, since nothing says which is right) and against the table, which makes re-running the same file harmless.
regexp_match returns the captured groups or NULL. A date that isn't DD.MM.YYYY, an ISO date included, yields NULL instead of a guess. Numbers lose their thousands dots and get a decimal point.

A cast runs only when pg_input_is_valid says it will succeed, so the view itself can never raise an error: 31.11.2026 fits the pattern but isn't a date. The regex insists on Turkish grouping, so 1.250,5 is 1250.5 and a bare 1.250 would be 1250, never 1.25.
KALDI is accepted thanks to the Turkish collation; Gecti, typed without the ç, is rejected rather than guessed at.

Report first. A view is evaluated on every read: after the INSERT the good rows are in test_runs and would come back as "already imported". One statement with a data-modifying CTE also works, since all its parts see the same snapshot.

examples.title: COPY ON_ERROR ignore, LOG_VERBOSITY and REJECT_LIMIT, and what they miss

annotations.note: TC-3 (month 13) and TC-4 (decimal comma) fail type conversion. TC-2 doesn't: under MDY, 09.11.2026 is a perfectly good September 11.
Pinned so the example gives the same result on every server; the point stands for whatever DateStyle yours has.
Skipped rows are reported as NOTICEs, which pgx hands to OnNotice rather than returning them from CopyFrom. The line numbers count the header line.

ON_ERROR ignore (PG 17) skips rows whose values fail conversion, and the tag counts only what was loaded: COPY 3 of 5. Without verbose you get just the summary notice; LOG_VERBOSITY silent (PG 18) drops that too.
REJECT_LIMIT (PG 18): the second bad row exceeds the limit of 1 and the whole COPY fails as if ignore weren't there. A guard for feeds: skip the odd bad row, refuse a file that is mostly garbage.
ignore covers conversion errors only. A CHECK violation or a missing column still aborts the whole COPY, and nothing from that file is loaded, not even TC-1.
TC-2 sits in the table as 2026-09-11. ON_ERROR can tell bad syntax from good, not a wrong value from a right one; that takes rules, which is what the staging view is for.

use_cases: Importing test results, requirement lists or price lists that people export from Excel, with an error report they can act on
Nightly feeds from another system: stage, validate, move, and keep the rejects for someone to look at
Loading into a table with row-level security, which COPY FROM doesn't support: COPY into staging, then INSERT ... SELECT
Machine-generated files where an occasional malformed row may be dropped: COPY with ON_ERROR ignore and a REJECT_LIMIT
strengths: Every rule sees the whole file and the real tables at once: duplicates within the file and references to existing rows are one EXISTS or window function, where a Go or Python loop would have to load the lookup tables first
Collects every problem of every row in one pass, unlike COPY or a constrained INSERT, which stop at the first error
The soft checks (pg_input_is_valid) use the server's own parsers, so a value that passes is exactly what the column will accept
Bad rows never touch the real table: no dead rows from a failed load, no partially imported file
weaknesses: The data is written twice (staging, then target); for very large, trusted feeds, COPY straight into the table is faster
Every constraint of the target has to be mirrored as a rule, and the two can drift apart when the schema changes
SQL regexes and CASE chains get long; messages meant for end users (and in Turkish) are easier to build in application code
ON_ERROR ignore is quick but blind: it reports bad rows only as NOTICEs and lets wrong-but-parseable values through

pitfalls.title: Casting DD.MM.YYYY straight to date
pitfalls.detail: The result depends on DateStyle: 03.04.2026 becomes March 4 on a server with MDY. Match the pattern and build an ISO date.
pitfalls.good:
SELECT make_date(d[3]::int, d[2]::int, d[1]::int)
FROM staging, regexp_match(run_on, '^(\d\d)\.(\d\d)\.(\d{4})$') AS d;

pitfalls.title: Treating "valid" as "correct"
pitfalls.detail: pg_input_is_valid('1.250', 'numeric') is true, and the value is 1.25. Check the Turkish format with a regex before converting, so the dot is read as a thousands separator.

pitfalls.title: lower() without the Turkish collation
pitfalls.detail: Under the default case rules KALDI lowers to kaldi, which matches no label. Apply tr-x-icu, or compare against a fixed list of accepted spellings.
pitfalls.bad: CASE lower(result) WHEN 'kaldı' THEN false END
pitfalls.good: CASE lower(result COLLATE "tr-x-icu") WHEN 'kaldı' THEN false END

pitfalls.title: Expecting ON_ERROR ignore to clean a file
pitfalls.detail: It skips type-conversion failures only. A CHECK, NOT NULL, unique or foreign key violation still aborts the whole COPY, and values that parse but mean something else (09.11.2026 under MDY) go straight in.

pitfalls.title: Reading the validation view after the move
pitfalls.detail: The view re-runs its checks on every read; once the clean rows are in the target, they look like duplicates. Report before moving, do both in one statement, or store the verdicts in a staging column.

quiz.q: With DateStyle = 'ISO, MDY', what does SELECT '03.04.2026'::date return?
options: An error: the format is ambiguous
quiz.why: Ambiguous day/month input follows DateStyle's field order, and MDY reads 03 as the month. Nothing warns you.

quiz.q: COPY ... WITH (FORMAT csv, ON_ERROR ignore) reads 1,000 rows; row 500 violates a CHECK constraint. What ends up in the table?
options: 1,000 rows, with row 500's value set to NULL
quiz.why: ON_ERROR only applies to errors converting input values to column types. A constraint violation aborts the statement as usual.

quiz.q: Why collect the problems in an array instead of a CASE that returns the first failing rule?
options: A row can break several rules, and the user should see them all in one report
quiz.why: array_remove(ARRAY[...], NULL) keeps every reason that applies; a single CASE stops at its first true branch.

quiz.q: In a UTF-8 database with default case rules, which expression maps both KALDI and Kaldı to 'kaldı'?
quiz.why: Only Turkish case rules lower I to dotless ı; the default rules give kaldi.

body:
## Concept

Never `COPY` a file from people straight into the table it belongs in. Use three steps:

1. **Load** the file into a staging table whose columns are all `text`, with no
   constraints, plus a row number. `\copy` in psql or `PgConn().CopyFrom` in Go. The
   load can't fail on content, so every line arrives.
2. **Validate** with one query, usually a view: compute the typed value of each field (or
   NULL), and a list of problems per row. Formats are checked with regular expressions,
   "would this cast work?" with `pg_input_is_valid` (PG 16), references with `EXISTS`
   against the real tables, duplicates within the file with a window function, and
   duplicates against the target with `EXISTS` again.
3. **Move and report**: `INSERT ... SELECT` the rows without problems, and give the
   others back to the user with their row numbers and reasons.

Whether a bad row means "skip it" or "refuse the whole file" is a policy decision, and
both are one `WHERE` clause away: the example imports the clean rows; adding
`AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT FROM checked WHERE problems <> '{}')` makes it all or nothing.

COPY's own alternative is `ON_ERROR ignore` (PG 17), with `LOG_VERBOSITY verbose`
to name the skipped rows and `REJECT_LIMIT` (PG 18) to cap them. It skips rows whose
values fail type conversion and nothing else: no format rules, no references, no
duplicates, no CHECK constraints.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Python/pandas**: `read_csv(dtype=str)` followed by `pd.to_numeric(errors="coerce")`
  is the same shape: everything as text first, then a conversion that yields a missing
  value instead of raising. `pg_input_is_valid` is that `errors="coerce"`, in SQL.
- **Java**: Bean Validation reports every constraint violation of an object, not the
  first. The `problems` array does that for every row of a file in one query.
- **TS**: zod's `safeParse` returns all issues instead of throwing (see
  `ts.services.zod`); a staging view is `safeParse` over a whole table.
- **Go**: the `go.files-io.csv-json` lesson validates per field while reading with
  `csv.Reader`. That is the better place for format checks with exact line and column
  positions; SQL is better at the rules that need other rows: duplicates and
  references, checked without loading lookup tables into Go.
- **ETL tools** (SSIS, Talend): their "error output" of rejected rows is here just the
  rows `WHERE problems <> '{}'`.

## How it works

Staging as text works because conversion is where COPY and INSERT fail fast. A text
column accepts any string, and with no constraints there is nothing else to violate.
The checks then use functions that report instead of raising: `pg_input_is_valid(text,
type)` returns false where the cast would throw, and `pg_input_error_info` returns the
message, detail and SQLSTATE it would have thrown. Both take a type name with modifiers,
such as `'numeric(6,2)'`, so they also catch overflow. The docs note they only work this
way for types whose input function reports soft errors; the built-in date and numeric
types used here do.

Three Turkish traps sit in this path. Dates: an ambiguous date like `03.04.2026` is read
in DateStyle's field order (built-in default `ISO, MDY`, though initdb picks one from
the server locale); `YYYY-MM-DD` input means the same everywhere. Numbers:
PostgreSQL only reads a decimal point, and `1.250` is a valid number with a different
meaning. Case: `lower` and `upper` follow the collation, and only Turkish rules (`COLLATE
"tr-x-icu"`) map I to ı and İ to i.

For real loads, the staging table can be `TEMPORARY` (private to the session, dropped
at its end) or `UNLOGGED` (no write-ahead log, so faster, but emptied after a crash).
Either fits data you can reload from the file. COPY can fill staging from a Turkish
Excel file directly:
`\copy staging (case_code, req_code, run_on, seconds, result) FROM 'kosular.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER true, DELIMITER ';', ENCODING 'WIN1254')`.

## Design notes

Keep the verdicts. A staging table with an `import_id` and a `problems` column filled
by `UPDATE ... FROM checked` survives the request, so the UI can offer the rejected
rows as a CSV with an extra "Hata" column, which is what people fixing a spreadsheet
actually want. Delete old imports on a schedule.

Mirror every constraint of the target as a rule, or the move can still fail as a
whole, but keep the constraints too: they are the guarantee, the rules are the error
messages. Two imports of the same file at the same moment can both pass the
"already imported" check; the primary key still stops the second one, and
`ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` in the move, or an advisory lock around the import (the
transactions module), turns that into a clean outcome.

Split the work by what each side is good at: the Go handler checks encoding, header
and field formats while it streams the upload and can point at line and column; SQL
checks what needs the database: references, duplicates, existing rows. Keep
`ON_ERROR ignore` for machine feeds where dropping the odd malformed row is acceptable,
and always give it a `REJECT_LIMIT`, so a feed that suddenly changed its format fails
instead of loading 3 rows out of 30,000.

files.examples/02_validate_move.sql:
CREATE TABLE requirements (code text PRIMARY KEY);
INSERT INTO requirements VALUES ('REQ-1'), ('REQ-2');
CREATE TABLE test_runs (
  case_code text         NOT NULL,
  req_code  text         NOT NULL REFERENCES requirements,
  run_on    date         NOT NULL,
  seconds   numeric(6,2) NOT NULL CHECK (seconds >= 0),
  passed    boolean      NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (case_code, run_on)
);
INSERT INTO test_runs VALUES ('TC-1', 'REQ-1', '2026-11-02', 4, true);

-- All text, no constraints: loading the file can't fail. In psql:
-- \copy staging (case_code, req_code, run_on, seconds, result) FROM 'kosular.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER, DELIMITER ';')
CREATE TABLE staging (
  row_no int GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY,
  case_code text, req_code text, run_on text, seconds text, result text
);
INSERT INTO staging (case_code, req_code, run_on, seconds, result) VALUES
  ('TC-2', 'REQ-1', '09.11.2026', '1.250,5', 'Geçti'), ('TC-3', 'REQ-2', '10.11.2026', '0,75', 'KALDI'),
  ('TC-4', 'REQ-9', '10.11.2026', '2', 'geçti'),       ('TC-5', 'REQ-1', '31.11.2026', '2,5', 'Gecti'),
  ('TC-6', 'REQ-2', '11.11.2026', '-1', 'Kaldı'),      ('TC-1', 'REQ-1', '02.11.2026', '4', 'Geçti'),
  ('TC-7', 'REQ-2', '12.11.2026', '3,1', 'Geçti'),     ('TC-7', 'REQ-2', '12.11.2026', '3,2', 'Geçti');

-- Every rule in one place: typed values, or NULL plus a reason.
CREATE VIEW checked AS
SELECT s.row_no, s.case_code, s.req_code, t.run_on, t.seconds, t.passed,
  array_remove(ARRAY[
    CASE WHEN NOT EXISTS (SELECT FROM requirements r WHERE r.code = s.req_code) THEN 'unknown requirement' END,
    CASE WHEN t.run_on IS NULL THEN 'date is not DD.MM.YYYY' END,
    CASE WHEN t.seconds IS NULL THEN 'bad number' WHEN t.seconds < 0 THEN 'negative seconds' END,
    CASE WHEN t.passed IS NULL THEN 'result is not Geçti/Kaldı' END,
    CASE WHEN count(*) OVER (PARTITION BY s.case_code, t.run_on) > 1 THEN 'twice in file' END,
    CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT FROM test_runs x WHERE (x.case_code, x.run_on) = (s.case_code, t.run_on))
         THEN 'already imported' END], NULL) AS problems
FROM staging s
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT regexp_match(s.run_on, '^(\d\d)\.(\d\d)\.(\d{4})$') AS d,
                           replace(replace(s.seconds, '.', ''), ',', '.') AS n) p
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT
  CASE WHEN pg_input_is_valid(p.d[3] || '-' || p.d[2] || '-' || p.d[1], 'date')
       THEN (p.d[3] || '-' || p.d[2] || '-' || p.d[1])::date END AS run_on,
  CASE WHEN s.seconds ~ '^-?(\d{1,3}(\.\d{3})+|\d+)(,\d+)?$' AND pg_input_is_valid(p.n, 'numeric(6,2)')
       THEN p.n::numeric(6,2) END AS seconds,
  CASE lower(s.result COLLATE "tr-x-icu") WHEN 'geçti' THEN true WHEN 'kaldı' THEN false END AS passed) t;

-- Report first, move second (see the note on why the order matters).
SELECT row_no, case_code, array_to_string(problems, '; ') AS problems
FROM checked WHERE problems <> '{}' ORDER BY row_no;

INSERT INTO test_runs (case_code, req_code, run_on, seconds, passed)
SELECT case_code, req_code, run_on, seconds, passed FROM checked WHERE problems = '{}';

SELECT * FROM test_runs ORDER BY run_on, case_code;
